word: A Man After His Own Heart
pronunciation: uh MAN AF-tur hiz OHN HART
pos: n. phr. (the LORD's description of David's successor, 1 Samuel 13:14)
etymology: Hebrew 'īsh kilbābō — a man according to His heart; lēbāb, the inner man, the seat of will and purpose rather than of sentiment.
biblical_def: Samuel says it to Saul at Gilgal, after Saul has forced himself and offered the burnt offering rather than wait the seven days appointed: But now thy kingdom shall not continue: the LORD hath sought him a man after his own heart, and the LORD hath commanded him to be captain over his people, because thou hast not kept that which the LORD commanded thee. The phrase is therefore first of all a verdict on Saul, and it is defined by the clause that follows it. A man after God's own heart is a man who keeps what the LORD commanded; the contrast is obedience against self-will, not warmth against coldness. It is not a certificate of superior character, and the man it named went on to commit adultery and arrange a murder. What distinguished David was what he did when confronted: Saul, caught, explained himself and blamed the people; David, caught, said I have sinned against the LORD and wrote the fifty-first Psalm. Paul repeats the description in the synagogue at Antioch and joins it to the same test — a man after mine own heart, which shall fulfil all my will. The Hebrew lēbāb is the seat of will and purpose, so the sense is a man whose intention runs with God's, who may fall badly and will not finally go his own way.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Heart, the seat of the affections and passions; also, disposition of mind, and the seat of the will. 1 Samuel 13:14, the man whose purpose runs with God's.
webster_full: Heart, the seat of the affections and passions; the will; the disposition of mind.
After, according to; in conformity with; as, a man after my own heart.
Captain, a head or chief officer; a commander; a leader.
Hebrew lēbāb, the inner man — mind, will, and purpose, not sentiment only.
Fulfil, to accomplish; to perform what is required. Acts 13:22.
scriptures: And Samuel said to Saul, Thou hast done foolishly: thou hast not kept the commandment of the LORD thy God, which he commanded thee: for now would the LORD have established thy kingdom upon Israel for ever.

But now thy kingdom shall not continue: the LORD hath sought him a man after his own heart, and the LORD hath commanded him to be captain over his people, because thou hast not kept that which the LORD commanded thee.

And when he had removed him, he raised up unto them David to be their king; to whom also he gave testimony, and said, I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after mine own heart, which shall fulfil all my will.
Psa 51:4
Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight: that thou mightest be justified when thou speakest, and be clear when thou judgest.
corruption_summary: The phrase is read as a compliment to David's temperament or emotional warmth, detached from the obedience the verse itself names; or it is used to excuse his sins as the acceptable cost of a passionate heart.
corruption_paragraphs: The sentimental reading makes David a man of feeling — the psalmist, the harpist, the one who danced before the ark — and takes the phrase as God's endorsement of expressive devotion. The text defines itself differently. Samuel speaks the words as the reason Saul's kingdom is torn away, and he ends the sentence with because thou hast not kept that which the LORD commanded thee. Paul, citing it, adds which shall fulfil all my will. The measure is obedience to the revealed command, and a devotional warmth that does not issue in it has not met the standard the verse sets.

The opposite abuse turns the phrase into a shield. Because David was a man after God's own heart and also an adulterer, it is argued that God is indifferent to such sins in those He has chosen, or that passion excuses them. Scripture is blunt in the other direction: the thing that David had done displeased the LORD, the child died, the sword never departed from his house, and he reaped in his own sons what he had sown. The doctrine to recover is the difference between a man who sins and repents and a man who sins and manages the consequences. Saul kept his throne for years and lost the kingdom; David lost nearly everything and kept the covenant, because when he was named he did not argue.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'īsh kilbābō, a man according to His heart — lēbāb is will and purpose, and the verse defines the phrase by obedience.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'īsh, a man; kilbābō, according to his heart.
Hebrew lēbāb, the inner man: mind, will, intention, resolve.
The clause that defines it: because thou hast not kept that which the LORD commanded thee.
Paul adds the test in Acts 13:22 — which shall fulfil all my will.
Hebrew nāgīd, captain or prince — the office David is appointed to.
usage: the LORD hath sought him a man after his own heart
because thou hast not kept that which the LORD commanded thee
a man after mine own heart, which shall fulfil all my will

word: There Is a Sound of Abundance of Rain
pronunciation: thair iz uh SOWND uv uh-BUN-duns uv RAYN
pos: n. phr. (Elijah to Ahab on Carmel, 1 Kings 18:41)
etymology: Hebrew qōl hamōn haggāshem — qōl, a voice or sound; hāmōn, a multitude, tumult or roar; geshem, the heavy downpour as distinct from the early and latter rains.
biblical_def: The fire has fallen, the prophets of Baal are slain, and the sky over Carmel is still empty after three years and six months without rain. Elijah says to Ahab, Get thee up, eat and drink; for there is a sound of abundance of rain. There was no sound. Elijah then climbs to the top of Carmel, casts himself down with his face between his knees, and sends his servant seven times to look toward the sea until a cloud the size of a man's hand appears. The order of events is the point: the prophet announces the rain before there is any evidence of it, and then prays as though everything depended on the praying. He had the word of the LORD — I will send rain upon the earth — and the word was his warrant to speak and his reason to pray, not an excuse to stop. James makes the episode the church's model of prayer and is careful to add that Elijah was a man subject to like passions as we are, lest the example be dismissed as prophetic privilege. The sound Elijah heard was the promise; the rain that came was the answer; and between the two lay seven refusals to give up.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Abundance, great plenty; an overflowing quantity. Sound, the perception of the ear; a noise. 1 Kings 18:41, the rain announced before any sign of it.
webster_full: Abundance, great plenty; an overflowing quantity; ample sufficiency.
Sound, that which is heard; a noise; the report of a thing.
Rain, water falling in drops from the clouds.
Hebrew geshem, a heavy rain or downpour; hāmōn, a roar or multitude.
Effectual fervent prayer, James 5:16-18, where Elijah is the instance given.
scriptures: And it came to pass after many days, that the word of the LORD came to Elijah in the third year, saying, Go, shew thyself unto Ahab; and I will send rain upon the earth.
And Elijah said unto Ahab, Get thee up, eat and drink; for there is a sound of abundance of rain.
And said to his servant, Go up now, look toward the sea. And he went up, and looked, and said, There is nothing. And he said, Go again seven times.
Jam 5:17
Elias was a man subject to like passions as we are, and he prayed earnestly that it might not rain: and it rained not on the earth by the space of three years and six months.
corruption_summary: The verse is made a proof text for naming blessings into existence by confident speech, which reverses its logic; or Elijah's praying is read as redundant beside the promise.
corruption_paragraphs: The word-of-faith and name-it-and-claim-it teachers have made this verse a showpiece: Elijah declared what he could not see and it came to pass, therefore the believer's confident declaration creates the outcome. The chapter will not support it. Elijah is not generating a result by speech; he is repeating what God had already told him in verse one of the same chapter, Go, shew thyself unto Ahab; and I will send rain upon the earth. The sound he heard was a promise given, not a reality summoned. Faith that has a word from God to stand on is the whole of the example, and a declaration with no such word behind it is presumption wearing faith's clothes. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: the entry names the word-of-faith formula in order to reject it

The opposite error treats the praying as theatre. If God had promised rain, why send the servant seven times? Because Scripture everywhere joins the decree to the means, and prayer is among the appointed means. Daniel read in Jeremiah that the seventy years were determined and immediately set his face to seek the LORD by prayer and supplications. The doctrine to recover is that a promise is a reason to pray and never a reason to stop, and that the man who prayed until the seventh look was not doubting the word but honouring it.
roots_summary: Hebrew qōl hāmōn geshem, the roar of a downpour — a promise heard before it is seen, and prayed through until it came.
roots_lines: Hebrew qōl, a voice or sound; here a sound no one else could hear.
Hebrew hāmōn, a multitude, tumult, or roaring abundance.
Hebrew geshem, the heavy rain, distinct from yōreh and malqōsh.
The warrant is the word already given in 1 Kings 18:1.
The servant is sent seven times before the cloud appears, 1 Kings 18:43.
usage: get thee up, eat and drink; for there is a sound of abundance of rain
go again seven times
Elias was a man subject to like passions as we are

word: The LORD Is Slow to Anger, and Great in Power
pronunciation: thuh LORD iz SLOH too ANG-gur and GRAYT in POW-ur
pos: n. phr. (Nahum's preface to the doom of Nineveh, Nahum 1:3)
etymology: Hebrew YHWH 'erek 'appayim — long of nostrils, the Hebrew idiom for slowness to anger, since the flaring nostril was the image of wrath; joined here to g'dol-kōach, great of power.
biblical_def: Nahum opens his burden against Nineveh with a line Jonah had quoted a century earlier as the reason he fled: the LORD is slow to anger. Nahum keeps the clause and adds two others — and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked. The combination is the whole doctrine. Slowness to anger is not reluctance born of weakness; it is the patience of One who has the power to act whenever He chooses and does not choose yet. Nineveh had repented under Jonah and had been spared, and the hundred and more years between that mercy and this burden are themselves the exhibit of the longsuffering Nahum names. Now the reprieve ends. The prophet sets the attribute in a passage of storm and earthquake — the LORD hath His way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of His feet — so that no reader can mistake patience for indifference. Two things are held together that men habitually pull apart: God delays, and God does not acquit. The delay is real mercy, offered to the city once and taken; the refusal to acquit is real justice, and it arrives on a schedule set by the same Person who set the delay.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Slow, not hasty; not precipitate; acting with deliberation. Acquit, to set free or judicially to clear from a charge. Nahum 1:3, patience and justice named in one sentence.
webster_full: Slow, not hasty; not rash or precipitate; acting with deliberation.
Acquit, to set free; to release from an obligation or a charge of guilt.
Power, ability to act; force; strength; the faculty of doing a thing.
Hebrew 'erek 'appayim, long of nostrils — the idiom for slowness to anger.
Hebrew nāqāh, to be clean or acquitted; here with the double negative. Nahum 1:3.
scriptures: Nah 1:2
God is jealous, and the LORD revengeth; the LORD revengeth, and is furious; the LORD will take vengeance on his adversaries, and he reserveth wrath for his enemies.
Nah 1:3
The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked: the LORD hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet.
Exo 34:6
And the LORD passed by before him, and proclaimed, The LORD, The LORD God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth,
The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance.
corruption_summary: Divine patience is turned into divine permissiveness, so that the delay is read as a change of mind; or Nahum's God of judgment is set against the God of the Gospels as a lower stage of revelation.
corruption_paragraphs: The commonest corruption is to take slowness to anger as the whole character and to treat the second half of the verse as an embarrassment. God is patient, therefore He will not finally judge — the inference that annihilationism and universalism both require and that much ordinary preaching assumes. Nahum puts the two clauses in one breath precisely to forbid it, and Peter does the same in the New Testament: the Lord is not slack concerning His promise, but longsuffering, not willing that any should perish — and then, the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night. Patience is the interval before the judgment, not its cancellation.

The second corruption is older and still current: Marcion's instinct, that the God of Nahum and the God of the Gospels are not the same, with the Old Testament's wrath assigned to a primitive stage of religion that Christ outgrew. The sentence Nahum quotes is itself the LORD's self-description from Sinai, proclaimed as He passed before Moses, and the New Testament has more to say about eternal judgment than the Old does, most of it from the lips of Christ. The principle to recover is that longsuffering and the refusal to acquit are the same attribute seen at two moments, and that a God who were only patient would not be good.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'erek 'appayim, long of nostrils — slow to anger because great in power, and for that reason unable to acquit the wicked.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'erek, long; 'appayim, nostrils — the idiom for patience under provocation.
Hebrew kōach, power or strength; the patience belongs to One who could act at once.
Hebrew nāqāh, to acquit or hold innocent; Nahum denies it absolutely.
The clause is quoted from the LORD's self-revelation at Sinai, Exodus 34:6.
Jonah had cited the same attribute as his reason for fleeing, Jonah 4:2.
usage: the LORD is slow to anger, and great in power
and will not at all acquit the wicked
the LORD hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm

word: Peace, Peace; When There Is No Peace
pronunciation: PEES PEES wen thair iz NOH PEES
pos: n. phr. (Jeremiah's charge against the false prophets, Jeremiah 6:14)
etymology: Hebrew shālōm shālōm w''ēn shālōm — the doubling is emphatic, the manner of a confident proclamation; shālōm is wholeness and welfare, not merely the absence of war.
biblical_def: The charge stands twice in Jeremiah, in the same words: They have healed also the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace. The figure is medical. A wound is treated on the surface, bound up and pronounced well while the infection goes on underneath, and the physician who does it is not merely mistaken but guilty, because the patient would have sought real help had he been told the truth. Jeremiah names the culprits exactly: from the prophet even unto the priest, every one dealeth falsely. These were not pagans but Judah's own clergy, saying what the people wanted and what the court rewarded, while Babylon marched. Ezekiel gives the same indictment a different image — a wall built badly and daubed with untempered morter, which looks sound until the overflowing shower brings it down. The sin is not optimism but false assurance: telling people they are at peace with God when they are not, and so removing the alarm that might have driven them to repent. The test Jeremiah applies is in the preceding verse: the false prophets were covetous and dealt falsely, and in the chapter before, the people loved to have it so.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Peace, a state of quiet or tranquillity; freedom from war; reconciliation with God. Slightly, superficially; with little care. Jeremiah 6:14, the wound healed on the surface.
webster_full: Peace, in a Scriptural sense, reconciliation with God; spiritual peace of conscience.
Peace, freedom from war, from agitation, or from disturbance.
Slightly, superficially; with little care; in a trifling manner.
Hebrew shālōm, wholeness, welfare, soundness, peace.
Untempered morter, Ezekiel 13:10, the daubing that cannot bear the shower.
scriptures: Jer 6:13
For from the least of them even unto the greatest of them every one is given to covetousness; and from the prophet even unto the priest every one dealeth falsely.
Jer 6:14
They have healed also the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace.
Jer 8:11
For they have healed the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace.
Because, even because they have seduced my people, saying, Peace; and there was no peace; and one built up a wall, and, lo, others daubed it with untempered morter:
corruption_summary: The rebuke is turned against any preaching of comfort at all, breeding a ministry of perpetual severity; or it is applied only to other men's pulpits while the same false assurance is given under gentler words.
corruption_paragraphs: The verse is a favourite with those who have concluded that a faithful ministry must always wound. But Jeremiah is not condemning the announcement of peace — the same book promises a new covenant, and the same prophet is told to build and to plant as well as to root out. He is condemning the announcement of peace where there is none. A preacher who cannot comfort the afflicted has not escaped the error; he has only reversed it, and the sufferer he leaves without the gospel is as badly served as the impenitent who is told all is well.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is how the thing actually happens now. Almost no one says the words; the false peace is given by omission — by a gospel presentation that never mentions sin, by a counselling that treats guilt as a feeling to be managed rather than a verdict to be answered, by the quiet retirement of judgment, hell and repentance from the ordinary diet of preaching. The daughter of Jeremiah's people was not told she was fine; she was told everything except what was wrong with her, which came to the same thing when Babylon arrived.
roots_summary: Hebrew shālōm doubled for emphasis — a confident proclamation of welfare over a wound healed only on the surface.
roots_lines: Hebrew shālōm, wholeness, soundness, welfare; more than the absence of war.
The doubling is the manner of confident public proclamation.
Hebrew rāphā', to heal; qālal, lightly or slightly — a superficial cure.
The same charge stands twice: Jeremiah 6:14 and Jeremiah 8:11.
Ezekiel's parallel figure is the wall daubed with untempered morter, Ezekiel 13:10.
usage: they have healed also the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly
saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace
from the prophet even unto the priest every one dealeth falsely

word: The Voice of the Bridegroom, and the Voice of the Bride
pronunciation: thuh VOYS uv thuh BRYD-groom and thuh VOYS uv thuh BRYD
pos: n. phr. (the fourfold refrain of Jeremiah, marking a land made desolate or restored)
etymology: Hebrew qōl chāthān w'qōl kallāh — chāthān, a bridegroom, from the root for contracting a marriage; kallāh, a bride or daughter-in-law.
biblical_def: Four times Jeremiah uses the same refrain, and the fourth reverses the first three. In chapters 7, 16 and 25 the LORD declares that He will cause to cease from the cities of Judah and from the streets of Jerusalem the voice of mirth, and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride, for the land shall be desolate. In chapter 33, with Jerusalem already under siege, the identical words return as promise: in this place of which ye say it is desolate, there shall be heard again the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride. The refrain is chosen with care. Weddings are the ordinary sound of a people with a future; a nation that has stopped marrying has stopped expecting one, and the silencing of that particular noise is the most domestic way Scripture has of describing judgment. Its restoration is therefore the most domestic way of describing mercy, and Jeremiah joins it to the promise of the Branch of righteousness and to the covenant that cannot be broken. Revelation takes the same refrain to its end: the voice of the bridegroom and of the bride is heard no more at all in Babylon, and is heard at the marriage supper of the Lamb.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Bridegroom, a man newly married, or about to be married. Bride, a woman newly married or about to be. Jeremiah's refrain for a land desolate, and for the same land restored.
webster_full: Bridegroom, a man newly married, or on the point of being married.
Bride, a woman newly married, or about to be married.
Mirth, social merriment; noisy gaiety; hilarity.
Hebrew chāthān, a bridegroom; kallāh, a bride or daughter-in-law.
Hebrew shābath, to cease or cause to cease. Jeremiah 7:34.
scriptures: Jer 7:34

Then will I cause to cease from the cities of Judah, and from the streets of Jerusalem, the voice of mirth, and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride: for the land shall be desolate.
Jer 16:9

For thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Behold, I will cause to cease out of this place in your eyes, and in your days, the voice of mirth, and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride.

The voice of joy, and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride, the voice of them that shall say, Praise the LORD of hosts: for the LORD is good; for his mercy endureth for ever: and of them that shall bring the sacrifice of praise into the house of the LORD. For I will cause to return the captivity of the land, as at the first, saith the LORD.

And the light of a candle shall shine no more at all in thee; and the voice of the bridegroom and of the bride shall be heard no more at all in thee: for thy merchants were the great men of the earth; for by thy sorceries were all nations deceived.
corruption_summary: The refrain is read as sentimental scene-setting rather than as covenant sanction and covenant promise, and its reversal in Jeremiah 33 is detached from the Branch who secures it.
corruption_paragraphs: Read as atmosphere, the line is merely a poignant way of saying that times were hard. It is in fact a covenant sanction. Deuteronomy had set out what obedience and disobedience would bring upon the land, and the silencing of ordinary joy is among the curses; Jeremiah is announcing the terms, not describing a mood. Where the covenant frame is lost, the fourth occurrence also loses its force, because the restoration of the sound is not optimism about the national temperament but the LORD keeping a promise He had bound Himself to keep.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is what Jeremiah 33 attaches the promise to. The voices return in the same breath as the Branch of righteousness raised up unto David and the covenant with day and night which cannot be broken — that is, the restoration of ordinary human gladness is grounded in the coming of Christ and in the immutability of God's word, not in a turn of political fortune. A people that wants its weddings back and does not want its Redeemer has misread the passage, and Revelation 18 shows where that road ends: a city in which the voice of the bridegroom is heard no more at all.
roots_summary: Hebrew qōl chāthān w'qōl kallāh — the wedding sound, silenced as covenant judgment and restored as covenant promise.
roots_lines: Hebrew qōl, voice or sound; chāthān, bridegroom; kallāh, bride.
Hebrew sāsōn, joy, and simchāh, gladness, stand with it in the refrain.
Three occurrences are judgment: Jeremiah 7:34, 16:9 and 25:10.
The fourth reverses them as promise: Jeremiah 33:11.
Revelation 18:23 applies the silencing to Babylon's fall.
usage: the voice of mirth, and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride
then will I cause to cease from the cities of Judah
the voice of them that shall say, Praise the LORD of hosts

pos: n. phr. (the foreigners joined to the LORD, Isaiah 56:6)
etymology: Hebrew b'nē hannēkār — sons of the foreignness; nēkār denotes what is foreign or alien, distinct from gēr, the resident sojourner already provided for in the Law.
biblical_def: Isaiah 56 opens the house of God wider than the returning exiles expected. The eunuch who keeps the sabbath is promised a name better than of sons and of daughters, and then: Also the sons of the stranger, that join themselves to the LORD, to serve him, and to love the name of the LORD, to be his servants, every one that keepeth the sabbath from polluting it, and taketh hold of my covenant; and then the promise — Even them will I bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer. The chapter ends with the sentence our Lord quoted when He cleansed the temple: mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people. Two guards keep the passage from being what it is often made. The welcome is not unconditional — it is given to those who join themselves to the LORD, love His name, keep His sabbath and take hold of His covenant, which is to say to converts, not to foreigners as such. And it is not a late innovation; Solomon had prayed at the dedication that the LORD would hear the stranger who came out of a far country for His name's sake. The passage is the Old Testament's plainest anticipation of the Gentile ingathering, and Paul's language of those who were afar off being made nigh by the blood of Christ is its fulfilment.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Stranger, a foreigner; one who belongs to another country. Join, to unite; to associate. Isaiah 56:6, the foreigner who takes hold of the covenant.
webster_full: Stranger, a foreigner; one who belongs to another country; one not a native.
Stranger, one unknown; a guest; one not admitted to communication or fellowship.
Join, to unite; to couple; to associate; to confederate.
Hebrew nēkār, that which is foreign or alien; distinct from gēr, a sojourner.
House of prayer for all people, Isaiah 56:7, quoted by Christ in Mark 11:17.
scriptures: Isa 56:3
Neither let the son of the stranger, that hath joined himself to the LORD, speak, saying, The LORD hath utterly separated me from his people: neither let the eunuch say, Behold, I am a dry tree.
Isa 56:6

Also the sons of the stranger, that join themselves to the LORD, to serve him, and to love the name of the LORD, to be his servants, every one that keepeth the sabbath from polluting it, and taketh hold of my covenant;
Isa 56:7

Even them will I bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer: their burnt offerings and their sacrifices shall be accepted upon mine altar; for mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people.
Eph 2:13
But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ.
corruption_summary: The passage is made a charter for admitting all comers on their own terms, with the covenant conditions Isaiah states quietly dropped; or it is confined to ethnic Israel's future and denied to the church.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern use of Isaiah 56 is as a text of unconditional welcome: God's house is open to everyone, full stop, and any requirement laid on the newcomer is read as the exclusion the chapter condemns. Isaiah says something more generous and more demanding. The sons of the stranger are brought to the holy mountain, and they are described in the same sentence as joining themselves to the LORD, serving Him, loving His name, keeping His sabbath and taking hold of His covenant. The welcome is real and it is to a covenant, not around one. What the chapter forbids is the man who has done all this being told he is still an outsider by blood; what it does not do is dispense with the joining.

The opposite error assigns the promise wholly to a future national Israel and withholds it from the church, which empties the chapter of the use the New Testament actually makes of it. Our Lord quoted verse seven against the traders in the court of the Gentiles — the very place where the sons of the stranger were to pray — and Paul tells the Ephesians that they who were sometime far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ, and are no more strangers and foreigners but fellowcitizens with the saints. The principle to recover is that the Gentile ingathering was promised in the prophets before it was accomplished in Acts, and that it was always a covenant ingathering.
roots_summary: Hebrew b'nē hannēkār, sons of the foreigner — brought to the holy mountain on the terms of joining, loving, keeping and taking hold.
roots_lines: Hebrew nēkār, foreignness or alien descent; b'nē hannēkār, its sons.
Distinguished from gēr, the resident sojourner of the Mosaic law.
Hebrew lāvāh, to join oneself, cleave to, be attached.
Hebrew chāzaq bab'rīth, to take hold of the covenant, Isaiah 56:6.
Solomon had prayed for the stranger from a far country, 1 Kings 8:41-43.
usage: the sons of the stranger, that join themselves to the LORD
every one that keepeth the sabbath from polluting it, and taketh hold of my covenant
mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people

word: He Shall Not Cry, Nor Lift Up, Nor Cause His Voice to Be Heard in the Street
pronunciation: hee shal not KRY nor LIFT UP nor KAWZ hiz VOYS too bee HURD in thuh STREET
pos: n. phr. (the manner of the Servant, Isaiah 42:2)
etymology: Hebrew lō' yits'aq w'lō' yissā' — tsā'aq, to cry out or raise an outcry, the word used of a public clamour; nāsā', to lift up, here of raising the voice.
biblical_def: The first of Isaiah's Servant songs opens with the Father's presentation — Behold my servant, whom I uphold; mine elect, in whom my soul delighteth — and then, before any account of His work, describes His manner. He shall not cry, nor lift up, nor cause His voice to be heard in the street. The point is not that the Servant will be silent; He preached in synagogues, on a mountain, from a boat, and in the temple courts. The point is that He will not campaign. The street was where causes were advertised and partisans were gathered, and the Servant declines that whole method. The next verse continues in the same register: a bruised reed shall He not break, and the smoking flax shall He not quench. Matthew quotes the passage at a particular moment — after the Pharisees took counsel to destroy Jesus, when He withdrew and healed the multitudes and charged them that they should not make Him known. The restraint is therefore deliberate and costly, not temperamental mildness. The same verse adds the clause that keeps it from being weakness: he shall bring forth judgment unto truth, and he shall not fail nor be discouraged, till he have set judgment in the earth.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Cry, to utter a loud voice; to clamour. Street, a public way in a city. Isaiah 42:2, the Servant who will not advertise His cause.
webster_full: Cry, to utter a loud voice; to speak with vehemence; to clamour.
Street, a public way or road in a city or village.
Lift up, to raise; of the voice, to speak aloud or vehemently.
Hebrew tsā'aq, to cry out, raise an outcry, call for help publicly.
Hebrew nāsā', to lift, bear, or raise up. Isaiah 42:2.
scriptures: Isa 42:1
Behold my servant, whom I uphold; mine elect, in whom my soul delighteth; I have put my spirit upon him: he shall bring forth judgment to the Gentiles.
Isa 42:2
He shall not cry, nor lift up, nor cause his voice to be heard in the street.
Isa 42:3
A bruised reed shall he not break, and the smoking flax shall he not quench: he shall bring forth judgment unto truth.
He shall not strive, nor cry; neither shall any man hear his voice in the streets.
corruption_summary: The verse is made a rule of perpetual quietism that forbids public contending for the truth, or it is reduced to a note on Christ's personality rather than a description of His method.
corruption_paragraphs: Taken as a general rule, the verse has been used to rebuke every public stand: the Servant did not raise His voice in the street, therefore neither should His people. The same Servant drove the traders out of the temple with a scourge, pronounced eight woes on the scribes and Pharisees to their faces, and sent His disciples to preach upon the housetops what they had heard in the ear. Isaiah is not forbidding plain public speech; he is describing a Messiah who will not take the kingdom by agitation, faction or display. The men of Jerusalem expected a deliverer who would do exactly that, and the verse is written against their expectation, not against the preaching of the gospel.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the restraint here is strength under orders. Matthew quotes the passage precisely where Christ withdraws from men plotting His death and heals quietly instead, and the quotation runs on to the clause that He shall not fail nor be discouraged till He have set judgment in the earth. The Servant's refusal to shout is not the absence of a verdict but the deferral of it; judgment is coming, and the One who declined to advertise Himself will bring it forth unto victory.

word: He Was Oppressed, and He Was Afflicted, Yet He Opened Not His Mouth
pronunciation: hee wuz oh-PREST and hee wuz uh-FLIK-tid yet hee OH-pund not hiz MOWTH
pos: n. phr. (the silence of the Suffering Servant, Isaiah 53:7)
etymology: Hebrew niggas w'hū' na''aneh w'lō' yiphtach-pīw — nāgas, to press, drive or exact as a taskmaster does; 'ānāh, to be bowed down or afflicted.
biblical_def: The verse stands at the centre of the fourth Servant song and reports not what was done to the Servant but how He bore it: He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth. The silence is the thing Isaiah dwells on, repeating the clause at both ends of the sentence. Two images carry it. The lamb led to slaughter is the paschal victim and the daily offering, going without resistance; the sheep before her shearers is dumb not from terror but from a strange submission. The Gospels record the fulfilment with evident care. Before Caiaphas, Jesus held His peace until put upon oath; before Herod, who questioned Him in many words, He answered nothing at all; before Pilate, He answered never a word, insomuch that the governor marvelled greatly. The silence is not stoicism and not helplessness. He had said that He could pray to His Father and have twelve legions of angels, and that no man took His life from Him. Peter draws the pastoral conclusion for the suffering church: when He was reviled, He reviled not again; when He suffered, He threatened not; but committed Himself to Him that judgeth righteously.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Oppress, to crush by hardship or severity. Afflict, to give pain to; to grieve. Isaiah 53:7, the Servant silent before His accusers.
webster_full: Oppress, to crush by hardship, severity, or unreasonable exactions.
Afflict, to give pain of body or mind; to grieve; to trouble.
Dumb, mute; silent; not speaking.
Hebrew nāgas, to press, drive, exact, as a taskmaster.
Hebrew 'ānāh, to be bowed down, humbled, or afflicted. Isaiah 53:7.
corruption_summary: The silence is made a model of passive endurance of all injustice, or it is read as the resignation of a victim rather than the deliberate act of One laying down His life.
scriptures: Isa 53:6
All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.
Isa 53:7
He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth.
And he answered him to never a word; insomuch that the governor marvelled greatly.
Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously:
corruption_paragraphs: The verse has been used to teach that the believer must never answer a charge, and more damagingly to tell the wronged that silence is always the Christlike course. Scripture itself answers. Paul appealed unto Caesar, stood on his Roman citizenship, and told the council plainly that God would smite the whitewashed wall; our Lord Himself, struck by an officer, asked why He was smitten. The silence of Isaiah 53 is specific: it is the silence of a substitute under a sentence He has agreed to bear. Where a man is bearing another's penalty by consent, there is nothing to say; where he is simply being wronged, Scripture permits him to speak.

The second corruption reads the Servant as a victim whose dignity lies in enduring what He could not prevent — a figure for all innocent sufferers and nothing more. Isaiah will not allow it. The same chapter says that it pleased the LORD to bruise Him, that He made His soul an offering for sin, that He bare the sin of many, and that He poured out His soul unto death; and John records His own words, that no man taketh His life from Him but He layeth it down of Himself. The principle to recover is that the silence was priestly, not merely patient. He said nothing because there was nothing to plead: the charge He was answering was ours.

Hebrew 'ānāh, to be afflicted, bowed down, humbled.

Two figures: the lamb to the slaughter and the sheep before her shearers.

pos: n. phr. (the gospel invitation of Isaiah 55:1)
etymology: Hebrew hōy kol-tsāmē' — hōy is the herald's interjection, elsewhere the cry of woe, here the cry of summons; tsāmē', thirsty, from the root for thirst.
biblical_def: Isaiah 55 opens as a street cry: Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price. The form is a market summons and the content contradicts the market, for the terms are no money and no price. Three things define the invitation. Its reach is every one, with no limit of nation or standing. Its only qualification is thirst — not worth, not preparation, not money, but want; and the next verse presses the point by asking why they spend money for that which is not bread. And its cost is nothing to the buyer, which is not to say nothing at all, since the chapter before has just described the Servant who made His soul an offering for sin. The invitation is immediately joined to a command: Seek ye the LORD while he may be found, call ye upon him while he is near: and then — Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts: and let him return unto the LORD, and he will have mercy upon him. Free does not mean unconditional in the sense of requiring no repentance; it means unpurchasable. Revelation closes the canon with the same offer in almost the same words: whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Ho, an exclamation used to call the attention of a person at a distance. Thirst, a painful sensation occasioned by the want of drink. Isaiah 55:1, the free invitation.
webster_full: Ho, an exclamation used to call the attention of a person at a distance.
Thirst, the pain or uneasiness occasioned by the want of drink; eager desire.
Buy, to acquire property by paying a price; here, without money and without price.
Hebrew hōy, the herald's interjection; elsewhere the cry of woe.
Hebrew tsāmē', thirsty; the only qualification named. Isaiah 55:1.
scriptures: Isa 55:1
Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.
Isa 55:2

Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not? hearken diligently unto me, and eat ye that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness.
Isa 55:7
Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts: and let him return unto the LORD, and he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon.
And the Spirit and the bride say, Come. And let him that heareth say, Come. And let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely.
corruption_summary: The freeness of the offer is taken to mean that nothing is required of the sinner at all, so that repentance is read out of the chapter; or the offer is narrowed until it is no longer made to every one.
corruption_paragraphs: The chapter is a favourite with those who preach a grace that asks nothing, and the first two verses can be made to sound that way if the seventh is left unread. Isaiah does not leave it unread. Six verses after the invitation he commands the wicked to forsake his way and the unrighteous man his thoughts and to return unto the LORD. The water is without price and the drinking is not without repentance, and the two have never been in competition: the man who has nothing to pay is exactly the man who must stop pretending he has, which is what forsaking his own way means.

The opposite narrowing is a real danger in a confessionally Reformed dictionary and must be named. Because the atonement is definite and the elect are a particular people, some have concluded that the gospel offer may not honestly be made to every one. Isaiah 55:1 is Ho, every one, Revelation 22:17 is whosoever will, and our Lord's own invitation is to all that labour and are heavy laden. The free offer of the gospel to all without exception, pressed sincerely, stands alongside the particularity of the atonement in the historic Reformed confessions and in the Puritans who preached them. The principle to recover is that the preacher is not the accountant of election; he is the herald, and his text begins with Ho.

word: Break Forth Before You Into Singing
pronunciation: BRAYK FORTH bee-FOR yoo IN-too SING-ing
pos: n. phr. (the creation's welcome of the redeemed, Isaiah 55:12)
etymology: Hebrew yiphts'chū liphnēkem rinnāh — pātsach, to break out or burst forth, used of a sudden loud sound; rinnāh, a ringing cry, of joy or of supplication.
biblical_def: Isaiah closes the great invitation chapter with the manner of the return from exile: For ye shall go out with joy, and be led forth with peace: the mountains and the hills shall break forth before you into singing, and all the trees of the field shall clap their hands. The figure is of creation itself greeting the redeemed as they pass. It is not mere decoration. Scripture holds that the ground was cursed for man's sake, that the creation was made subject to vanity not willingly, and that it groans and travails together until now, waiting for the manifestation of the sons of God. If the creation fell with man, it is fitting that it should rejoice at his deliverance, and Isaiah's next verse makes the link explicit by reversing the curse's own emblems: instead of the thorn shall come up the fir tree, and instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle tree. The singing mountains are therefore a statement about the scope of redemption. What Christ purchased is not the rescue of souls out of a doomed world but a new heaven and a new earth, and the hills that break forth into singing are the first sound of it. The verse ends by naming the purpose: it shall be to the LORD for a name, for an everlasting sign that shall not be cut off.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Break forth, to burst out; to issue suddenly. Singing, uttering melodious sounds. Isaiah 55:12, creation greeting the redeemed on their way home.
webster_full: Break forth, to burst out; to issue or come forth suddenly.
Sing, to utter sounds with musical inflections or modulations of voice.
Clap, to strike together with a quick motion, so as to make a noise.
Hebrew pātsach, to break out, burst forth into sound.
Hebrew rinnāh, a ringing cry of joy; also of entreaty. Isaiah 55:12.
scriptures: For ye shall go out with joy, and be led forth with peace: the mountains and the hills shall break forth before you into singing, and all the trees of the field shall clap their hands.
Instead of the thorn shall come up the fir tree, and instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle tree: and it shall be to the LORD for a name, for an everlasting sign that shall not be cut off.
Rom 8:21
Because the creature itself also shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God.
Psa 98:8
Let the floods clap their hands: let the hills be joyful together
corruption_summary: The line is read as poetic ornament with no doctrine in it, or it is annexed to a nature-mysticism in which the creation is itself divine or self-redeeming.
corruption_paragraphs: Treated as ornament, the singing mountains are a pleasant flourish and the verse teaches nothing. Isaiah is making a claim. The creation is bound up with man's standing before God — cursed at his fall, groaning under the vanity it did not choose, and delivered at his redemption — and Paul states the same doctrine in plain prose in Romans 8. Where the claim is dropped, Christian hope quietly shrinks to the escape of the soul from the world, which is Plato's hope and not Isaiah's.

The opposite error annexes the verse to a reverence for nature in its own right, in which the earth is a living mother to be heard and heeded, and redemption is the restoration of a balance rather than the work of a Redeemer. Isaiah forecloses it in the next breath: the transformation is the LORD's doing, it is to the LORD for a name, and the trees do not sing of themselves but before the people whom He is leading out. The principle to recover is that the creation is a creature. It sings at the right time, for the right reason, and about Someone else.
